speechtext:
It does not matter to me whether they be public or private companies. An important principle is involved here, which is that knowledge be supplied to the investors of this country. Confidence must be established in the integrity of issues that come onto the market in this country. There is no better way of achieving this than to have total and absolute disclosure by all companies in Canada.
I do not know whether the hon. member would raise the question that securities commissions, on the whole, tend to look at new issues rather than those of existing companies-though they do both, of course-and therefore there is a greater, perhaps overriding need for only new companies who are seeking support to be investigated rather than the long-established companies. I hope that is not his argument because there is considerable evidence that some long-established companies have had problems in this regard.
In the United States there are at the moment some of the most prestigious companies associated with the stock market either on the verge of or already in bankruptcy, and there is considerable investor disillusionment with some of the major institutions. I find it difficult to make a distinction between scrutiny and publication on the basis of whether a company has recently entered the money market or has been long established. I therefore do not see justification for creating a commission rather than making provision in a corporations act.
I also had difficulty with the hon. member's suggestion that provincial governments be involved in a matter of this kind. I think it would pose considerable problems for us. Constitutionally, I think the argument is quite sound that in matters of securities the provinces must be consulted. They have to be involved, and perhaps we will not be able to do anything unless this is so. At the practical level, experience has shown that the federal government has, on the whole, been more willing to work for things like disclosure, intelligent reporting and publication than have the provinces. The provinces find themselves taking different views. Some provinces are quite satisfied with things as they are; others are not so satisfied.
There is always a tendency for provinces that need development in the worst possible way to start a "beggar be thy neighbour" program-a program of outbiding everybody else, whether in the area of granting special concessions or not, or being lax about what they insist their investors should disclose, and things of that kind. In this kind of encounter, what happens is that those who want to take a stronger and firmer position are often

November 16, 1970
National Securities Commission reduced to a compromise which takes into account the lowest common denominator in order to reach agreement. This is always a factor when one is trying to seek agreement. However, it should be recognized as one of the practical defects of reaching agreement on something as important as disclosure and investor confidence.
I am of the view-I think there are others in the House of a similar view-that it may be more realistic and perhaps more practical for the federal government to take the lead. I know each time this is suggested others say that the provinces may not go along with the government, and this is true. What is more, they do not have to go along with the government. But when the federal government has taken the lead and has put forward legislation, at least respecting federally incorporated companies, ultimately the provinces have gone along with it and have adapted themselves to the circumstances.
[DOT] (5:40p.m.i
I think we can point to later legislation in this regard; for instance, minimum wages. We can also point to the Corporations Act, although in that case one province led the way rather than the federal government. I say these things in order to point out the importance of the federal government on its own asserting a point of view and asking the provinces to go along with it. It has the right to do this. The federal government does not have the power to compel the provinces to follow suit. I think the ability and the willingness to set an example would be emulated by others.
As willing as I am and as desirable as I think it might be to have this motion go to committee for examination, I think the effect of the motion would be to make the enforcement of safety regulations more difficult for the reasons I have enumerated. There is a necessity to get provincial co-operation because of a movement away from firm legislation, and a commission approach would not be as determined as it should be. I would be much more in favour of a motion calling for a federal-provincial conference on the Corporations Act and having in it suggestions incorporating full disclosure and full publication within the ambit of the Corporations Act, rather than having a commission type of organization.

subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITIES COMMISSION
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CONFERENCE WITH PROVINCE LEADING TO OPERATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for the motion he has placed before the House this afternoon. I sympathize with him in trying to draft a motion such as this one, because it involves a matter primarily within the responsibility of the provinces yet it is one of national concern and involves a national need. If the action he proposes could be taken, it would be to the national good. The possibility of achieving this action does not he in a private member's public bill but with a national conference through which, by publicity, pressure could be brought to bear on provincial governments which have the responsibility but are reluctant to give it up to the federal government. In this connection I understand there was a federal-provincial conference held in 1968, as the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) has men-
[Mr. Saltsman.l
tioned, at which there was considerable agreement between the federal government and the province of Ontario although little agreement among the other provinces concerned.
The hon. member's motion suggests that there be established a national securities commission controlled by the two levels of government, federal and provincial. In order to iron out the details as to how it might work, the hon. member suggests there should be held a national plenary conference. Few people would argue about the necessity for a national securities commission. Certainly there is need for a uniform standard of protection for investors throughout the country.
The provinces down through history have been reluctant to give up any of their fields of responsibility including property, civil rights and, in this case, provincial securities. Back in the late 1930's the provinces did agree to a constitutional amendment which made it possible to set up the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They gave up some of their rights there. They have at various times of national emergency given up their rights in the field of taxation, or at least agreed to turn them over to the federal government. However, they are very reluctant to do this. I think the strategy of the hon. member for Edmonton West in calling for a national plenary conference would establish a good forum in which to bring national publicity to the question and bring public opinion to bear, thereby putting pressure on provincial governments to give up some of their powers in this field so that something to the national good might be achieved in every part of the country.
How might we establish a national securities commission? It seems obvious that this is desirable. It could be composed of commissioners appointed by Governor in Council who would be responsible through the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to Parliament. Contrary to what the hon. member for Edmonton West has suggested, I would envisage the headquarters of this commission to be in Ottawa. He has suggested it should perhaps be in Toronto, which has the largest stock exchange. If this were done it would delay any agreement by other, small commissions throughout the country and provincial governments. They do not want to see control going to one of the other provincial capitals. I suggest the headquarters should be in Ottawa with strong regional offices, if necessary, to which the commissioners could travel from time to time as their duties required. The commission would be responsible under the federal securities act, and its powers would include the power to make regulations, carry out investigations and hear appeals.
The commission would be responsible for all international and provincial issues of and trading in any securities. Qualification of issues would be through the regional offices. A simple qualification procedure could be introduced for smaller issues. I think this would be an improvement, because some of the provincial commissions and governments were reluctant in 1968 to agree to the establishment of a national securities commission; they thought it might dampen down their ability, espe-
November 16, 1970

cially a province like British Columbia, to raise large issues of securities. The commission could also be responsible for other functions within the competence of Parliament, for example, the registering of investment dealers and brokers engaged in international or interprovincial issues of or trading in securities.
Having regard to the important matter of co-operation between federal and provincial authorities, there appear to be at least three possibilities. A province might wish to retain the administration of its own legislation. However, once federal legislation was passed it would necessarily prevail in regard to interprovincial and international offerings and tradings. I believe the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton suggested it was the view of the Ontario government that it should retain its own administration. On the other hand, the province might wish to delegate the entire field of securities administration to the federal securities commission, in which case the commission would, after certain conditions had been worked out, administer that province's securities legislation in addition to dealing with the federal securities act.
It might be possible to take a middle course by which the staff of the provincial commission and the federal securities commission would be merged. The federal securities commission and the provincial commission would remain distinct and separate bodies and the staffs of the two official bodies would have a dual function, one to administer the federal securities act in the province and the other to administer the provincial act. In exercising either of these two functions they would be responsible to the appropriate commission.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Two of the main advantages of the CANSEC proposal would then be realized. The knowledge and experience of existing staffs would be used in a co-operative fashion for a common securities administration along the lines of either of the two courses which I have outlined, and would call for consultation with provincial governments by the federal government on the choice of the federal commission's chief administrative officer, such other officers as were appropriate, and on other matters of common concern. Where the pooling of staff was agreed upon, the chief administrative officer under a provincial commission might also be appointed the head of the federal commission's regional office if this were mutually agreed.
Over the course of time the federal securities commission would become a central source of information on all securities matters, which would be available to all provincial securities commissions. Studies of developments in the securities industry could be undertaken either jointly or by the federal securities commission and the results of these studies would also be made available to the provincial securities commissions. The federal government should develop these ideas in fuller detail in consultation with the provinces. The paramount objective of the federal government should be to achieve, by the simplest and most economical means available under our Constitution, a system of securities' regulation best suited to Canada's needs. In pursuing this objective the federal

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether there is any value in arguing with the position the minister has taken, in view of his attitude toward the amendments, but I want to take just two or three minutes to say that I am not in the slightest convinced by the minister's argument that this is not retroactive legislation.
I am not going to take much time in dealing with the question of reverse onus represented by the last lines of clause 8. As I said this afternoon, we were not seeking to amend that. But much of what the minister said referred to the fact that the onus is placed on the accused to prove something that would discredit the earlier evidence against him. I am concerned merely with the question of retroactivity, and I say with the greatest respect to the minister that in his argument he was indulging in semantic legalisms.
Clause 8 is not the clause that provides the offence. It is true that the offence is provided in clause 4, and instead of having clause 8 here the minister could easily have added clause 8 as part of clause 4. That, surely, is irrelevant. What is relevant is that clause 8 sets out the facts under which a person is proven to be a member of the unlawful association, and being a member of the unlawful association is an offence against this law. Therefore, when you have proved that the person is a member of the unlawful association by reference to acts which occurred before the association was unlawful, you are making the substantive offence retroactive, and no number of words and no way of arguing will change that situation.
If I can be held to be a member of the FLQ today by virtue of the fact that I attended some meetings five years ago, then the law substantively is retroactive or retrospective. Certainly the retroactivity is in relation to the evidence on which I may be convicted, but this division between fact and law in this kind of situation seems to me to be entirely barren. When the minister referred to the fact that in an ordinary criminal case you can go back to acts, or action or behaviour of the accused prior to the date on which he is alleged to have committed the offence, you are dealing with something that has always been an offence. It has always been a crime to conspire to commit murder or to commit kidnapping. If I am alleged to have committed that crime on a certain date, and there is evidence prior to that date of my behaviour related to the crime with which I am charged, then of course it is admissible-not as evidence of the
charge as set out in the particulars but as evidence of my behaviour supporting that charge.
But this is a new offence. Membership in this organization was not unlawful before October 16. Attending a meeting of this organization was not proof of an unlawful act before October 16, nor was communicating on behalf of this unlawful organization an act which proved membership in an unlawful organization. It is this referral back to what I may have done a long time ago that is offensive.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Time and again in a number of clauses of this bill the minister has referred to the fact-and obviously it is a fact-that it is difficult to prove membership in the organization and that the FLQ is a clandestine organization. Presumably it has no membership card and no membership list, so the Crown would find it difficult to prove that anyone was a member. To extent this logic if it is difficult to prove membership of an organization it is almost equally difficult to disprove it, and in certain circumstances perhaps more difficult.
If there is no membership list and no membership card, it is not necessary to resign membership from the organization. If I am a member because I attend clandestine meetings of a cell or a group, how do I prove that I am no longer a member? I do not send in an official resignation and I do nothing to take me out of the organization of which I was a member. I have committed an offence merely because I attended a meeting some years ago of an organization that has now become unlawful. I have met many young Canadians in Quebec, mainly of French expression, who attended these meetings some time ago.

People who were, if you like, fooled by the social and economic objectives which the FLQ has always pretended were theirs and which existed before the bombings started. A young person may have attended a few such meetings six months ago, or four or five years ago, and be

November 16, 1970

charged under this law. The prosecution could then adduce evidence that he had attended those meetings. He may have spoken at them or advocated the purely social goals which the FLQ pretends to have. He may even have communicated FLQ manifestos to other people- manifestos which did not refer to terror, kidnapping or murder but merely dealt with the social and economic objectives of separating Quebec from Canada, of helping the unemployed, the poor and the dispossessed in the province of Quebec, or of fighting the authorities in Ottawa. A person in these circumstances who had attended the meetings or communicated the manifestos may find himself in court with witnesses for the Crown giving evidence of these facts. The prima facie, presumption as a result of these facts dating back six months or five years is that the person is a member of the FLQ and has the burden of disproving the allegation. I do not know how he can accomplish this. The point we wish to make is not merely the difficulty of the accused to disprove the awful and unjust situation in which he finds himself, but the wrongness of the principle of putting him in that position by making the law effectively retroactive even though the crime itself is not retroactive.
He is put in this position if the crime depends on acts which were entirely lawful at the time, and when the organization to which they were related was not unlawful except as a criminal or seditious conspiracy and, therefore, unlawful in the sense of the Criminal Code but not in the sense in which this bill makes it unlawful. This is the principle with which I am concerned. I have given the matter a great deal of thought since the bill was first introduced, as have all my colleagues. No amount of playing with words, differences between the evidentiary presumption or some other kind of presumption hides the fact that a person is presumed to be guilty because he is presumed to be a member of the organization. He then has to find some way of proving his innocence, and not the usual way where there is a shift of onus in the Criminal Code, because of acts committed when they were entirely lawful.
It is the retrospective aspect of this bill that we find entirely unacceptable, contrary to the basic principle of our criminal law, indeed of most of our law, and contrary to any concept of civil liberties and civil rights.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to my mind, clause 8, as it now stands, creates a simple presumption which, unless it was contradicted, would be enough to overrule a presumption of innocence. This, in itself, is not exceptional, because, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) pointed out this afternoon, the Criminal Code already contains quite a number of similar presumptions. Those presumptions hinge on past facts.
Nor is this remarkable in itself. The evidence of facts that preceded the crime is often accepted by the courts. With regard to clause 8, the danger lies in the retroac-
Public Order Act, 1970
tivity it may establish because of the vagueness of the expression "member of the unlawful association".
In effect, the act forbids membership in the association; clause 8 states how one can be proved a member but the act does not explain what it is to be a member. Obviously, according to the dictionary, "being a member" is the state of one who is part of an association; but as the "unlawful association" in question has no charter, no records, no membership cards, it is therefore very difficult to state specifically who can be a member of the said association. Therefore, it is normal to confuse the means of evidence outlined in clause 8 of the legislation, with the offence itself.
Thus, instead of merely being used as presumption, the facts enumerated in clause 8 will become the very basis of the offence. These presumptions concern past events which could have occurred even before membership in the FLQ was declared unlawful by law, as of October 16, at four o'clock in the morning. In that sense, the offence could be considered as having a retroactive effect.
I think the main issue is that the legislation seems to dismiss the possibility of a defence, in fact not in law, once the presumption is established. The phrase "un certain nombre de reunions" is much more indefinite than a certain number of meetings". In fact, the number "un" is a certain number, according to the Robert dictionary.
In my opinion, an exceptional legislation should be couched in the clearest possible terms. This is an example where the French and English terms do not have the same meaning. It is obvious that "a certain number" means "more than one" and that the French word "un" means "a certain number."
Now what happens to the persons who spoke on behalf of the unlawful association before October 16, at 4 a.m. and which were jailed under the regulations or the Criminal Code, after having been found guilty of criminal offences? The possibility that those individuals could be deprived of any legal means of defence makes us fear that the effect of that legislation could be retroactive.
If the proposed effect is really sought through the action of presumptions listed in the Criminal Code, we should add a clause describing what is meant by membership, which is not defined in the bill. I therefore move the following:
Is a member of the unlawful association any person whose participation in this association meets the requirements of the act for taking part in a seditious conspiration.
With this amendment, of course, the crime of being a member of an unlawfull association would be defined.
Also I do believe that failure to ascribe definitions to criminal acts is tantamount to enacting the Wrong kind of law, a law which is foreign to the principle of legality.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point which troubles me: once this legislation is passed, the commission of such acts as are listed under clause 8 would involve a presumption of membership in the association. Now it should be remembered that under clause 14, the fact that a person has on or after October 16 committed any of the

November 16, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
said acts, that is speaking publicly in favour of the association or communicating statements, amounts to an offence.
Then, in my opinion, telling a person that the fact that he has publicly spoken in favour of the association implies a dual offence, contravenes two widely admitted principles of criminal law:
Nemo bis vexari debet pro una et eadem causa, and Nemo debet bis punari pro uno delicto
I do not see how, especially after adoption of this act, the person who commits one of the offences can be accused at the same time of committing the other.
With regard to the retroactive effect of the act, it is not definite. Personally, I know several students who were previously members of the FLQ which had branches in several colleges around the years 1963-64, and who left this association when they found out that it was far from being patriotic. These persons, under this act, will be liable to arrest. The attorney general will be able to file a certificate with the clerk to this effect, under clause 7, and they will await their trial. Obviously, it can be said that acts of treason and of sedition are forbidden under the Criminal Code. However, this association became illegal only on October 16 at four o'clock in the morning. And people were arrested as soon as the regulations were enacted.
I understand why those persons cannot have violated the regulations: they were arrested in their sleep. Of course, today, we must have other remedies. As a solution, some suggest that we go back. While agreeing with the Minister of Justice that it is not exceptional in itself to establish presumptions for past actions, I feel that, taking into account the various factors I just mentioned, it is a bad technique. It is unthinkable that several provisions of the legislation should indicate how to determine membership in any association, that membership constitutes an offence and that it does not say what it is all about.
I think the minister is right once again in saying that we may go back. The theory of similar facts and other similar presumptions exists in the bill, but the way the clause is drafted, besides the error I pointed out to the effect that "un certain nombre" in French has not the same meaning as "a number of meetings", it seems to me that the act should be clearer.
I think this clause might be improved by being amended. I am aware of the impossibility refered to by the minister but I think it might have been possible-by including, for instance, the definition which I just suggested-to solve a good deal of the problems. I believe that any person who committed an unlawful act before October 16 is "indictable" under the Criminal Code. If we do not want to prosecute this person for the new offences which are obviously created here, I do not see why this legislation has, in some regards, a retroactive effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at one point I thought I would support the government when we came to consider
clause 8. When I spoke about our amendment I dealt with this particular clause. As it reads now, I agree with the minister that a question of evidence is involved. But it is a question of evidence which makes substantive law because it places the accused in a position where he is obliged to take the stand and defend himself. The minister can shake his head, but this is what will happen.
The Minister of Justice well knows that an accused has to be proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and the onus is on the Crown to so prove. But here the onus is placed squarely on the accused. In effect, this clause has made the law retroactive. The minister should refer to the case of Clarke v. The King and the other cases on this point; the citation is 25 Canadian Criminal Cases. The fact remains that in practice the implementation of clause 8 will force the accused to take the stand, which is contrary to normal procedure. Laymen who listen to television shows think the accused always takes the stand. We do not act like Perry Mason. We do not walk up to the bench to whisper to the judge. We do not act as they do in that television show. We do not put the accused on the stand to solve every case. It has been my experience and the experience of other defence lawyers that very rarely is the accused put on the stand, regardless of his guilt or innocence. The reason is that he is then subject to cross-examination. He may leave some doubt as to his innocence in the minds of the jury and therefore be convicted.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The onus is strictly on the Crown. That is the principle of British jurisprudence. This principle has been adopted throughout the Commonwealth, including Canada, and throughout the United States. The Minister of Justice referred to the Narcotic Control Act. As far as I am concerned, that is contrary to the Bill of Rights. Perhaps the courts will have something to say about that. There is the Income Tax Act. All these statutes are being set up by the Crown. They have similar clauses. They are different from the Criminal Code. The onus is shifted to the accused and the defence.
I agree with the Minister of Justice that this is a matter of evidence, but in practice it becomes substantive law. Once a person has attended four or five meetings of this association or has been associated with it in accordance with clause 8, and it is established he did this prior to October 16, he is guilty of the crime unless he takes the stand. What does this mean? When a person is arrested, under the normal rules of jurisprudence he does not have to make a statement. In fact, the police in the jurisdictions of the ten provinces have been instructed to warn an accused that anything he may say may be used against him at his trial. The minister tries to carry that over to this by saying, therefore, that if one attended meetings of the FLQ three or four years ago, prior to the time of the offence, which could only occur since October 16, that can be used against him. The point I make is that in all of these other laws under which a person's action prior to the time of the offence can be presumptive evidence against him, it was at least a crime at the time the offence was committed or the act was performed.
In this case we are being asked to say that what a person did when it was not illegal, when it was perfectly within the law, can be used as presumptive evidence against him in the period of time when the new law is in effect. I submit that the things my colleagues have said about the dangers of retroactive law of this kind are correct and that we are embarking on a dangerous course.
Perhaps I may go a bit further in respect of what I heard the minister say this afternoon. Mr. Chairman, there is a
good deal in this legislation which I find offensive. Perhaps there is little that is more offensive than the clause we are discussing. The decision to include a clause which would allow the police to arrest and charge people who have been members of a particular group or organization for some years and who perhaps a few weeks ago terminated that membership, all argument to the contrary, is something that is so unbelievable and unjust that I find it difficult to comprehend that any government would have the audacity to bring such a suggestion in legislative form before this House. I find it repugnant that members of this House should be expected to approve a clause of this bill which would establish guilt on a retroactive basis.
This clause states that membership of any nature in an organization that was not considered unlawful until a few weeks ago can constitute the necessary evidence with which to charge a person with a criminal offence. This is too strong and unpalatable to be justified on the ground of security in this country. Not only are we in effect stating that certain acts in the past which individuals may have committed, or certain statements which individuals may have made, are a crime, but in this legislation we are creating a new crime which is either membership in, support for or encouragement given to a particular movement.
This would be bad enough in itself in light of the traditions of this country, but the fact is that we have not yet been given evidence in these many days or weeks of debate concerning the nature of the FLQ and what in particular would constitute reasonable evidence in respect of a criminal offence in this respect. Certainly the minister did not offer to this House in the earlier discussion on clause 3, which was stood, nor in the subsequent debate on various other clauses any relevant information concerning the exact nature of what would constitute a crime in respect of the FLQ. I think he has not done it primarily because he is not able to do it.
In the first instance, the minister has not been able to define the exact nature of the FLQ for purposes of arrest, charge and conviction. Are we, then, to be asked to put ourselves in the completely unbelievable position of suggesting that attendance at meetings or earlier support for some aspects of this organization will constitute evidence that would convict one of a criminal offence? This really is an Alice in Wonderland situation. I am amazed at the audacity and the fictional kind of existence in which the minister and the government must live, when they would expect either members of this House or the people of the country to believe that the establishment of a clause establishing retroactivity is in the best interests of the country or in the best interests of dealing with the present difficulties in the province of Quebec.

Further, it is beyond me how we can in all justice expect to have the people of this country accept as fair legislation which calls for the establishment of criminal offences which when committed in the past were not criminal. By the simple passage of this clause in the bill we would in effect be telling the people that something they did in the past, which to the very best of their knowledge did not constitute a criminal offence, has now in fact become a crime.
It is possible that next year the government might decide that some other organization is in effect of a like nature to the FLQ, and that it would constitute a criminal offence to support that organization, not only now when the legislation becomes valid but perhaps 10, 15 or 20 years ago when it seemed to be no criminal offence to belong to or support a specific organization. It is incredible that we should be engaging in a discussion of such a proposal this evening. Although we certainly are dealing with an organization which is repugnant to almost 100 per cent of the population today, this does not set aside the possibility that some other day another government, or perhaps this government, will propose similar steps in respect of other organizations, other activities, other bodies and other beliefs or ideologies.
In this proposal we are asked to accept a presumption of guilt which strikes me as being contrary to everything I understand of our system of justice. A person will be called upon to prove that in his earlier association, which he may have terminated half dozen years ago, he has no longer maintained some kind of active interest or support. How in the name of heaven is an innocent individual before the courts expected to prove the nebulous assertion that he is no longer an active member or supporter of that particular organization?

There is one thing that is basic to the legislative framework assembled in this place. Not only must we provide laws that are just and fair to the citizenry of this country; they must, above all else, appear to be just. 2. In any prosecutions for the offence of being a member of the unlawful association, the accused shall not be convicted unless it is established that he knew of the use of force or the commission of crime by members of the unlawful association.

If we are to accept the minister's interpretation of clause 8, it is that this is an evidentiary presumption in relation to the one offence of membership in the FLQ. This afternoon he outlined how the presumption operates. If the accused can set forth a case with the balance of probabilities in his favour, then the onus shifts to the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is a member of the FLQ. But the thing that concerns me, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure it concerns members of the faculty of Osgoode Hall law school of York University, is that there are two types of membership, active and passive.
Clause 8 of the bill states:

In paragraph (a) you have participation in or being present, in paragraph (b) you have speaking publicly in advocacy for the unlawful association, and in paragraph (c) you have communicating a statement on behalf of or as a professed representative of the unlawful association. The first line of paragraph (a) states, "participated in or was present at a number of meetings", but you get an active participation in the other paragraphs. Under paragraph (a) you could have a charge against a person who "participated in or was present at". When you look at the words "was present at" it means you are sort of dwelling on mere membership.

If a person is charged under clause 4 with being a member and the evidence comes forth that he was present at a number of meetings-the minister has said this may be an improvement over the regulations-the question arises as to the type of evidence he can present to rebut this allegation. It would be difficult for him to say, "I was not present at the meetings". The minister has admitted that there may be two types of evidence: he may be able to argue that he was not present, or that at the time of the charge or previous to it he had renounced membership in the association. I am sure this is the reason why the professors of Osgoode Hall at York University were so concerned about mere membership.

We are not dealing here with a person who is a member. The purpose of clause 8 is to prove that he is a member.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The minister dealt with participation, he dealt with advocacy and he dealt with communication. What the hon. member for Broadview was pointing out, so neatly sidestepped by the minister, was that any person who was present at a number of meetings of an unlawful association or a branch or committee thereof, or in attendance at meetings of a small group which did not put up big signs saying "this is the FLQ. Come in and get a machine-gun because we are people of violence," is a member of an unlawful association unless he can provide evidence to the contrary.
The hon. member for Broadview is pointing out, not that membership does not presume guilt but that mere attendance could be the result of a misadventure on the part of a person who attended a couple of meetings some years ago during student days and later became aware of the purposes and objectives of the organization and terminated his association with it. If the minister leaves this matter with the mere presence of someone at a meeting being proof of membership, and places that kind of power in the hands of attorneys general and police forces, he will have many cases of flagrant maladministration of justice in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will try to repeat again perhaps more succinctly, if I am able, what I said initially in reply to the hon. member for Broadview. It is no longer true to say that clause 8 can be interpreted without some ingredient of conscious action by way of participation or association at a number of meetings, or a course of conduct, or active communication, advocacy, promotion or something like that. That positive act assumes some conscious knowledge of what is going on.
I said that it was inconceivable to me that anyone who was a member of the FLQ, or attended meetings of the FLQ in such a fashion that he would be caught on a
November 16, 1970

presumption, would be someone other than one who attended meetings where they were discussing violence and sedition or, armed seditious violence. On the basis of common experience it is inconceivable to me, based on the notoriety of the FLQ, that anyone who was at such meetings would not know of their objectives and purposes.
I said to the hon. member for Broadview that in the hypothetical case where that might happen and where, on the basis of the accused's credibility before a jury or a judge he was able to satisfy the court or jury that that was so, I doubt very much if a jury or judge would convict, or if there were a conviction whether the sentence would amount to much. By adding the words the hon. member seeks to add, he in effect imposes an additional burden of proof on the Crown which I feel would be impossible to satisfy.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just one word at this time. The minister said several times earlier, in reply to hon. member's questions, particularly the questions of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, that the meeting would be an FLQ meeting at which there would be discussion of the aims of the FLQ and the unlawful means that group intended to use. If that is the case, why is my hon. friend's amendment so difficult? Obviously the Crown will have to prove-I am using the minister's own words-not only that there was a meeting, but that there was a meeting of a certain kind at which they advocated violence toward certain political ends. So the Crown would have to prove presence at that meeting, as well as the nature of the meeting. If it proved the nature of the meeting and I was there, obviously I ought to have known that the purpose of the FLQ was violence and crime. Surely this is logical.
The minister simply cannot argue, as he did before, that this amendment places an impossible burden upon the Crown. It has to prove the nature of the meeting and, therefore, that the meeting dealt with the unlawful act or the advocacy of it. If it proves that and the person was there, then obviously that person knew or ought to have known about it. The value of the amendment is in relation to some young person who was roped into attending a meeting; the meeting did not discuss violence; the meeting or a number of meetings discussed separating Quebec from Canada, fighting the battle of the unemployed, helping the poor in east Montreal, or whatever. This student or other young Canadian sits in at that meeting and is attracted to the slogans. He returns and attends another meeting or meetings where exactly the same kind of thing is discussed. But present at this meeting-I will mention names everybody knows-are Vallieres and Gagnon. The Crown will then say that Vallieres and Gagnon were charged with such-and-such and that it was after this the young man attended those meetings.
It is that kind of situation with which my friend's amendment would deal. This young Canadian who was roped into attending such a meeting innocently, and who listened to the social objectives in which the FLQ claims to have an interest, not knowing of the criminal inten-
Public Order Act, 1970
tions which may have been in the minds of the people or some of the people who may have been there, should not be subject to conviction and should not be the victim under this law. I do not see where the burden on the Crown is so difficult under the elements of the amendment of the hon. member for Broadview.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the basis of the hypothetical situation adduced by the hon. member, the accused undoubtedly would escape on the basis of the general wording. What I say to him-I can say it to him because of his legal experience and the sharpness of his mind-is that the burden of proof sought to be added by the hon. member for Broadview would either be impossible to discharge in one circumstance or redundant in the other. That capsulizes the reply I have been trying to make.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister is hanging his whole case on the fact that if a person attends an FLQ meeting, or a number of FLQ meetings, this means that person is familiar with the objectives and the means which the FLQ intends to use to attain those objectives. This does not necessarily follow at all. People have been attending Liberal meetings for years and still do not know the real purposes of the Liberal party.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to introduce such an amendment one has to be completely unaware of what terrorist movements are, the goals they seek and how they want to achieve them. In fact, the very essence of the FLQ, the MLQ or any other terrorist movement is their secrecy. Why? Because they seek to overthrow the government by violence.
Therefore, as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out this afternoon, we are not dealing with a political party. There are no membership cards and no contributions. These movements do not hold conventions, but secret meetings where terrorism is discussed.
That is pretty well known in the province of Quebec. The record of the FLQ is not recent, for since 1963, its members would have committed about 100 bombings, armed robberies or arms thefts, and they would have caused train derailments.
For those who do not know what the FLQ is, simply by attending one meeting of that association they can figure out how far those guys are willing to go. They state publicly and openly that murders have to be committed.

November 16, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
Everyone knows that in the province of Quebec. Several public meetings, which were not necessarily FLQ meetings, took place. Known supporters of the FLQ were sometimes in attendance at these meetings, indirectly as guests, or because they thrust themselves on a group, meeting for apparently peaceful purposes, to state that political leaders have to be assassinated. If FLQ members now dare say in public that political assassination must be used, there is every reason to suppose in view of the bombings, the robberies, the train derailments, and so on that in more secret meetings these people do not talk about overthrowing the government by democratic, legitimate and peaceful means.
Therefore I think that one would have to be a little naive and ill-informed about life in Quebec to imagine that someone could not know that the FLQ, the MLQ or any other similar movement is not a revolutionary movement attempting to overthrow the government by violence.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
I could not disagree more with the remarks that have just been made. Let me give a personal example of the point the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was trying to make. About two weeks ago I was speaking in Toronto and ran into a student who had recently attended five meetings of a Maoist group. He did not find out until the fifth meeting that it was either a Maoist group or that it believed in violence. This is not a foolish young man. He happens to be a first or second year student who is concerned about poor people in the city of Toronto. He was taken in, if you like to put it that way, by someone he thought was a well meaning student, quite innocent of violent politics, who got him to come out to some study groups. The study groups met a number of times. No mention was made of violence or of Communism, but finally at the
fifth meeting he discovered it was a Maoist group and immediately got out.
I think that is the point at issue, and it cannot be dismissed so readily. We are talking in this bill not only about the FLQ but about some successor, some related body, and it is indeed possible that well-meaning young people in the province of Quebec or elsewhere could attend a number of meetings without knowing about the real purposes of that organization.
